claim: The adenosine A2A receptor (A2AR) is a prototypical G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that couples to the heterotrimeric G protein GS.
source: The adenosine A2A receptor (A2AR) is a prototypical G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that couples to the heterotrimeric G protein GS.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about A2AR classification and coupling specificity.

claim: The structure of A2AR at pH 7.5 bound to NECA and coupled to an engineered heterotrimeric G protein was determined by electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM).
source: Here, we determine the structure by electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) of A2AR at pH 7.5 bound to the small molecule agonist NECA and coupled to an engineered heterotrimeric G protein, which contains mini-GS, the βγ subunits and nanobody Nb35.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental determination of the structure.

claim: Most regions of the A2AR-G protein complex have a resolution of ~3.8 Å or better.
source: Most regions of the complex have a resolution of ~3.8 Å or better.
evidence: Resolution is reported from the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The receptor and mini-GS in the cryo-EM structure are virtually identical to those in the 3.4 Å resolution crystal structure.
source: Comparison with the 3.4 Å resolution crystal structure shows that the receptor and mini-GS are virtually identical and that the density of the side chains and ligand are of comparable quality.
evidence: Direct comparison between cryo-EM and crystal structures is reported.

claim: The cryo-EM density map indicates regions that are flexible in comparison to the crystal structures, including regions in the ligand binding pocket.
source: However, the cryo-EM density map also indicates regions that are flexible in comparison to the crystal structures, which unexpectedly includes regions in the ligand binding pocket.
evidence: Flexibility is inferred from the quality of density in different regions of the map.

claim: An interaction between intracellular loop 1 of the receptor and the β subunit of the G protein was observed.
source: In addition, an interaction between intracellular loop 1 of the receptor and the β subunit of the G protein was observed.
evidence: The interaction is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A2AR is an archetypical Class A G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR).
source: The adenosine A2A receptor (A2AR) is an archetypical Class A G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2013).
evidence: Classification is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A2AR is activated by the endogenous agonist adenosine.
source: A2AR is activated by the endogenous agonist adenosine and plays a prominent role in cardiac function, the immune system and central nervous system, including the release of the major excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate (Fredholm et al., 2001; Fredholm et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A2AR plays a prominent role in cardiac function, the immune system and central nervous system, including the release of glutamate.
source: A2AR is activated by the endogenous agonist adenosine and plays a prominent role in cardiac function, the immune system and central nervous system, including the release of the major excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate (Fredholm et al., 2001; Fredholm et al., 2011).
evidence: Physiological roles are supported by citations.

claim: A2AR is a validated drug target for many disorders including Parkinson's disease and cancer.
source: Given the widespread tissue distribution and physiological relevance of A2AR, it is a validated drug target for many disorders (de Lera Ruiz et al., 2014), including Parkinson's disease (Hickey and Stacy, 2012) and cancer (Leone et al., 2015).
evidence: Drug target validation is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A2AR is one of the most stable GPCRs.
source: A2AR is one of the most stable GPCRs and structures have been determined of A2AR in an inactive state bound to inverse agonists (Doré et al., 2011; Jaakola et al., 2008; Congreve et al., 2012; Hino et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Segala et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2017), an active intermediate state bound to agonists (Lebon et al., 2015; Lebon et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011) and the fully active state bound to an agonist and coupled to an engineered G protein, mini-GS (Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: Stability is stated and supported by the extensive structural characterization cited.

claim: Structures of A2AR have been determined in an inactive state bound to inverse agonists.
source: A2AR is one of the most stable GPCRs and structures have been determined of A2AR in an inactive state bound to inverse agonists (Doré et al., 2011; Jaakola et al., 2008; Congreve et al., 2012; Hino et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Segala et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2017), an active intermediate state bound to agonists (Lebon et al., 2015; Lebon et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011) and the fully active state bound to an agonist and coupled to an engineered G protein, mini-GS (Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: Multiple citations support the existence of these structures.

claim: Structures of A2AR have been determined in an active intermediate state bound to agonists.
source: A2AR is one of the most stable GPCRs and structures have been determined of A2AR in an inactive state bound to inverse agonists (Doré et al., 2011; Jaakola et al., 2008; Congreve et al., 2012; Hino et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Segala et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2017), an active intermediate state bound to agonists (Lebon et al., 2015; Lebon et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011) and the fully active state bound to an agonist and coupled to an engineered G protein, mini-GS (Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: Multiple citations support the existence of these structures.

claim: Structures of A2AR have been determined in the fully active state bound to an agonist and coupled to mini-GS.
source: A2AR is one of the most stable GPCRs and structures have been determined of A2AR in an inactive state bound to inverse agonists (Doré et al., 2011; Jaakola et al., 2008; Congreve et al., 2012; Hino et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Segala et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2017), an active intermediate state bound to agonists (Lebon et al., 2015; Lebon et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011) and the fully active state bound to an agonist and coupled to an engineered G protein, mini-GS (Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation supports the existence of this structure.

claim: Structure-based drug design has been applied to inactive state structures of A2AR to develop potent and subtype specific inverse agonists with novel scaffolds.
source: In addition, structure-based drug design has been applied to inactive state structures of A2AR to develop potent and subtype specific inverse agonists with novel scaffolds (Congreve et al., 2012) and these are currently in clinical trials.
evidence: Citation supports the drug design application and clinical trial status is stated.

claim: Inverse agonists developed through structure-based drug design for A2AR are currently in clinical trials.
source: In addition, structure-based drug design has been applied to inactive state structures of A2AR to develop potent and subtype specific inverse agonists with novel scaffolds (Congreve et al., 2012) and these are currently in clinical trials.
evidence: Clinical trial status is stated as current fact.

claim: Mini-GS is an engineered G protein with eight point mutations and three deletions, including the whole of the α-helical domain.
source: The active state was determined by crystallizing the receptor coupled solely to mini-GS, an engineered G protein with eight point mutations and three deletions, including the whole of the α-helical domain (Carpenter and Tate, 2016).
evidence: The engineering details are stated and supported by citation.

claim: Mini-GS recapitulates the ability of a heterotrimeric G protein to increase the affinity of agonist binding to the receptor.
source: Although pharmacologically mini-GS recapitulates the ability of a heterotrimeric G protein to increase the affinity of agonist binding to the receptor (Carpenter et al., 2016), the roles for the βγ subunits could not be described.
evidence: Pharmacological characterization is supported by citation.

claim: The vast majority of interactions between a heterotrimeric G protein and a Class A GPCR are made by the α subunit, in particular the C-terminal α5 helix.
source: In terms of the interactions between a heterotrimeric G protein and a Class A GPCR, the vast majority of interactions are made by the α subunit, in particular the C-terminal α5 helix (Rasmussen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: There was an interaction between the β subunit and the β2-adrenoceptor.
source: However, there was an interaction between the β subunit and the β2-adrenoceptor (Rasmussen et al., 2011) and also between the β subunit and the class B receptors for calcitonin (Liang et al., 2017) and glucagon-like peptide (Zhang et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation supports the observation of this interaction.

claim: There was an interaction between the β subunit and the class B receptors for calcitonin and glucagon-like peptide.
source: However, there was an interaction between the β subunit and the β2-adrenoceptor (Rasmussen et al., 2011) and also between the β subunit and the class B receptors for calcitonin (Liang et al., 2017) and glucagon-like peptide (Zhang et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations support the observation of these interactions.

claim: There is mutagenesis data suggesting that the α2-adrenergic receptor directly interacts with the β subunit.
source: In addition, there is mutagenesis data suggesting that the α2-adrenergic receptor directly interacts with the β subunit (Taylor et al., 1994; Taylor et al., 1996).
evidence: Citations support the mutagenesis data.

claim: The Volta phase plate (VPP) enhances the probability of getting structural data of small proteins.
source: This is now possible given the recent developments in the field over the last few years (Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres, 2016) together with the improved contrast provided by the recently developed Volta phase plate (VPP) (Danev et al., 2014), which enhances the probability of getting structural data of small proteins (Khoshouei et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations support the capability of VPP.

claim: The A2AR construct used contained thioredoxin at the N-terminus of the receptor.
source: In this work, we used a construct of A2AR that contained thioredoxin at the N-terminus of the receptor (Nehmé et al., 2017).
evidence: The construct design is stated and supported by citation.

claim: The presence of thioredoxin did not significantly affect the pharmacology of A2AR.
source: The presence of thioredoxin did not significantly affect the pharmacology of A2AR, as assessed by determination of its apparent KD for the inverse agonist ZM241385 or in agonist shift assays (Figure 1).
evidence: Pharmacological characterization data is presented in Figure 1.

claim: Detergent-solubilised A2AR coupled to the heterotrimer had a molecular weight (excluding the detergent micelle of LMNG) of approximately 135 kDa.
source: Detergent-solubilised A2AR coupled to the heterotrimer had a molecular weight (excluding the detergent micelle of LMNG) of approximately 135 kDa (Nehmé et al., 2017).
evidence: Molecular weight is stated and supported by citation.

claim: The apparent KD for ZM241385 binding to A2AR is 0.5 ± 0.1 nM.
source: (a) Saturation binding of the inverse agonist 3H-ZM241385 to A2AR constructs gave the following apparent KDs: A2AR (circles), 0.5 ± 0.1 nM; TrxA-A2AR (squares), 0.8 ± 0.2 nM.
evidence: Binding data is presented in Figure 1.

claim: The apparent KD for ZM241385 binding to TrxA-A2AR is 0.8 ± 0.2 nM.
source: (a) Saturation binding of the inverse agonist 3H-ZM241385 to A2AR constructs gave the following apparent KDs: A2AR (circles), 0.5 ± 0.1 nM; TrxA-A2AR (squares), 0.8 ± 0.2 nM.
evidence: Binding data is presented in Figure 1.

claim: The Ki for NECA binding to A2AR is 1.0 ± 0.5 µM.
source: (b) Competition binding curves measuring the displacement of 3H-ZM241385 with increasing concentrations of NECA gave the following Kis for NECA; A2AR (filled circles), 1.0 ± 0.5 µM; A2AR + mini-GS (open circles, dashed line), 2.6 ± 1.8 nM; TrxA-A2AR (filled squares), 1.1 ± 0.4 µM; TrxA-A2AR + mini-GS (open squares, dashed line), 1.8 ± 1.2 nM.
evidence: Competition binding data is presented in Figure 1.

claim: The Ki for NECA binding to A2AR + mini-GS is 2.6 ± 1.8 nM.
source: (b) Competition binding curves measuring the displacement of 3H-ZM241385 with increasing concentrations of NECA gave the following Kis for NECA; A2AR (filled circles), 1.0 ± 0.5 µM; A2AR + mini-GS (open circles, dashed line), 2.6 ± 1.8 nM; TrxA-A2AR (filled squares), 1.1 ± 0.4 µM; TrxA-A2AR + mini-GS (open squares, dashed line), 1.8 ± 1.2 nM.
evidence: Competition binding data is presented in Figure 1.

claim: The Ki for NECA binding to TrxA-A2AR is 1.1 ± 0.4 µM.
source: (b) Competition binding curves measuring the displacement of 3H-ZM241385 with increasing concentrations of NECA gave the following Kis for NECA; A2AR (filled circles), 1.0 ± 0.5 µM; A2AR + mini-GS (open circles, dashed line), 2.6 ± 1.8 nM; TrxA-A2AR (filled squares), 1.1 ± 0.4 µM; TrxA-A2AR + mini-GS (open squares, dashed line), 1.8 ± 1.2 nM.
evidence: Competition binding data is presented in Figure 1.

claim: The Ki for NECA binding to TrxA-A2AR + mini-GS is 1.8 ± 1.2 nM.
source: (b) Competition binding curves measuring the displacement of 3H-ZM241385 with increasing concentrations of NECA gave the following Kis for NECA; A2AR (filled circles), 1.0 ± 0.5 µM; A2AR + mini-GS (open circles, dashed line), 2.6 ± 1.8 nM; TrxA-A2AR (filled squares), 1.1 ± 0.4 µM; TrxA-A2AR + mini-GS (open squares, dashed line), 1.8 ± 1.2 nM.
evidence: Competition binding data is presented in Figure 1.

claim: Initial micrographs without VPP reached 6.7 Å resolution after 3D classification and refinement.
source: After 3D classification and refinement, the best model (containing 72,486 particles) reached 6.7 Å resolution and showed clearly defined α-helices in both the receptor and G protein (Figure 2a).
evidence: Resolution is reported from data processing and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Images collected with a VPP possess higher contrast.
source: Since images collected with a VPP possess higher contrast (Figure 2b and c), the auto-picking feature in RELION that uses a Gaussian blob as a reference resulted in optimal particle picking without the need for specific 'auto-picking' references (Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres, 2017).
evidence: Higher contrast is observed in Figure 2b and c compared to 2a.

claim: Refinement of K2 Summit VPP data yielded a model with overall resolution of 4.88 Å.
source: After 2D and 3D classification (see Materials and methods for details), refinement yielded models with overall resolution of 4.88 Å and 4.45 Å for the K2 Summit and Falcon III detector, respectively (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Resolution is reported from refinement and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Refinement of Falcon III VPP data yielded a model with overall resolution of 4.45 Å.
source: After 2D and 3D classification (see Materials and methods for details), refinement yielded models with overall resolution of 4.88 Å and 4.45 Å for the K2 Summit and Falcon III detector, respectively (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Resolution is reported from refinement and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Falcon III model was later improved to 4.11 Å with further processing.
source: The Falcon III model was later improved to 4.11 Å with further processing (see below) showing details for most amino acid side chains after B factor sharpening.
evidence: Improved resolution is reported from additional processing.

claim: The effect of the VPP for this dataset was essential to make 'side-chain' resolution accessible.
source: The effect of the VPP for this particular dataset was therefore essential to make 'side-chain' resolution accessible.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of resolution with and without VPP.

claim: In the presence of the VPP, the A2AR map has a better resolution for the same number of particles and the B-factor improves significantly from 426 to 170.
source: It is observed that, in the presence of the VPP, the A2AR map not only has a better resolution for the same number of particles, but the B-factor improves significantly from 426 to 170 (when comparing K2 Summit with and without VPP).
evidence: B-factor comparison is shown in Figure 2e.

claim: To obtain 4.88 Å resolution using the K2 Summit detector without the VPP would have needed about 5 million particles, requiring ~65 days of data collection.
source: As an example, to obtain the same resolution of 4.88 Å using the K2 Summit detector without the VPP, one would have needed about 5 million particles, that would require ~65 days of data collection at a Titan Krios electron microscope (in comparison to 145,169 particles collected in 48 hr with a VPP).
evidence: This is calculated based on the B-factor plot analysis.

claim: The highest resolution data set corresponded to micrographs collected on a Falcon III detector in electron counting mode using a VPP.
source: The highest resolution data set corresponded to micrographs collected on a Falcon III detector in electron counting mode using a VPP, therefore this map was used for further processing, model building and subsequent analysis.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of the different datasets.

claim: 3D classification revealed that around 50% of the particles contained a heterogeneous γ subunit.
source: Attempts to improve the model included further 3D classification, which revealed that around 50% of the particles contained a heterogeneous γ subunit.
evidence: This is observed from 3D classification analysis.

claim: The overall resolution of the final model was estimated to be 4.5 Å, but the core of the complex was ~3.8 Å with most of the map at 4.0 Å resolution or higher.
source: Calculation of the local resolution in RELION showed that although the overall resolution was estimated to be 4.5 Å the core of the complex was ~3.8 Å with most of the map at 4.0 Å resolution or higher, with clearly visible density for the majority of amino acid side chains.
evidence: Local resolution calculation is performed on the cryo-EM map.

claim: The regions that showed poorer resolution were the thioredoxin and the detergent micelle.
source: As shown in Figure 3, the regions that showed poorer resolution were the thioredoxin and the detergent micelle (a significant fraction of the small complex), which hinders a realistic overall resolution estimation.
evidence: Local resolution map in Figure 3 shows these regions have poorer resolution.

claim: Refinement of signal subtracted particles (without micelle and thioredoxin) yielded an improved map at 4.11 Å resolution.
source: Refinement of these particles yielded an improved map at 4.11 Å resolution.
evidence: Resolution is reported after signal subtraction and refinement.

claim: The A2AR cryo-EM complex structure provides insights into its structure in solution, in the absence of crystal contacts and at more physiological conditions (pH 7.5) than the X-ray structure (pH 5.7 or below).
source: The A2AR cryo-EM complex structure provides insights into its structure in solution, in the absence of crystal contacts and at more physiological conditions (pH 7.5) than the X-ray structure (pH 5.7 or below for inactive structures).
evidence: This is inferred from the different experimental conditions of cryo-EM vs crystallography.

claim: The density map of the A2AR–G protein heterotrimer displayed a local resolution varying from 3.3 Å to 6.4 Å.
source: The density map of the A2AR–G protein heterotrimer displayed a local resolution varying from 3.3 Å to 6.4 Å (Figure 3).
evidence: Local resolution is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Side chain densities were observed for most amino acid residues and were of similar quality to those in the X-ray crystallographic map of the A2AR–mini-GS structure.
source: Side chain densities were observed for most amino acid residues (Figure 4), which were of similar quality to those in the X-ray crystallographic map of the A2AR–mini-GS structure (Figure 5).
evidence: Comparison of density quality is shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The lowest resolution was found at the C-terminus of the β subunit and most of the γ subunit, which had very poor density.
source: The lowest resolution was found at the C-terminus of the β subunit and most of the γ subunit, which had very poor density.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The C-terminus of the β subunit and most of the γ subunit region are flexible.
source: Upon implementation of these strategies, we did not find any other discrete conformations of the heterotrimeric G protein, suggesting that the C-terminus of the β subunit and most of the γ subunit region are flexible.
evidence: Flexibility is inferred from the absence of discrete conformations in 3D classification.

claim: Within the cryo-EM structure of A2AR, the N-terminal section of ECL2 (G147 to Q163) and the whole of ICL3 (E212 to S223) lack density and are probably disordered and flexible.
source: Within the cryo-EM structure of A2AR, there are two regions that lack density and are therefore also probably disordered and flexible, namely the N-terminal section of ECL2 (G147 to Q163) and the whole of ICL3 (E212 to S223).
evidence: Lack of density is observed in the cryo-EM map, suggesting disorder.

claim: Sections of the cryo-EM density map with poor quality density and high B-factors include TM1, helix 8, the second section of ECL2, ECL1 and ECL3.
source: Sections of the cryo-EM density map for which there is poor quality density and high B-factors of the refined coordinates include TM1, helix 8, the second section of ECL2 that contributes relevant residues for ligand binding (see below), ECL1 and ECL3 (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: Poor density and high B-factors are shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The overall architecture of the A2AR–heterotrimeric G protein complex is similar to the heterotrimeric GS-coupled complexes for the β2-adrenergic receptor, GLP1 and the calcitonin receptor.
source: The overall architecture of the A2AR–heterotrimeric G protein complex is similar to the heterotrimeric GS-coupled complexes for the β2-adrenergic receptor (Rasmussen et al., 2011), GLP1 (Zhang et al., 2017, Liang et al., 2018) and the calcitonin receptor (Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: Similarity is inferred from comparison with cited structures.

claim: The receptor and mini-Gs portions of the A2AR–G protein complex are very similar to the crystal structure of the A2AR–mini-GS complex, with the RMSD of Cα atoms for the receptor and mini-GS components being 0.5 Å and 0.6 Å, respectively.
source: The receptor and mini-Gs portions of the A2AR–G protein complex are very similar to the crystal structure of the A2AR–mini-GS complex, with the RMSD of Cα atoms for the receptor and mini-GS components being 0.5 Å and 0.6 Å, respectively.
evidence: RMSD values are calculated from structural comparison.

claim: The largest differences between cryo-EM and crystal structures are found at the interface between mini-GS and the β subunit.
source: The largest differences are found at the interface between mini-GS and the β subunit, which have a different conformation when βγ is bound.
evidence: Differences are observed from structural comparison.

claim: There is a minor difference in curvature of the α5 helix in mini-GS when it is in the heterotrimer complex compared to when it is bound to the receptor alone.
source: This may contribute to a minor difference in curvature of the α5 helix in mini-GS when it is in the heterotrimer complex compared to when it is bound to the receptor alone (Figure 5).
evidence: Difference in curvature is observed in Figure 5.

claim: The difference in α5 helix curvature does not have any major impact on the interface between the receptor and mini-GS.
source: However, this does not have any major impact on the interface between the receptor and mini-GS, thus further validating the use of mini G proteins as a surrogate for G protein heterotrimers (Carpenter et al., 2016; Carpenter and Tate, 2016; Nehmé et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison and supported by citations.

claim: The extracellular half of A2AR does not undergo any major structural changes in the transition from the active intermediate to the mini-GS coupled active state.
source: The extracellular half of A2AR does not undergo any major structural changes in the transition from the active intermediate to the mini-GS coupled active state, with the volume of the binding pocket remaining constant and the interactions to NECA being identical (Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural comparison.

claim: The orthosteric binding site in the cryo-EM map has well-defined density.
source: The orthosteric binding site in the cryo-EM map has well-defined density, although the map has lower resolution towards the extracellular surface.
evidence: Density quality is observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The density for NECA is of sufficient quality to allow an unambiguous orientation of NECA and the same interactions to the receptor are observed as present in the crystal structures.
source: The density for NECA is of sufficient quality to allow an unambiguous orientation of NECA and the same interactions to the receptor are observed as present in the crystal structures (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: NECA density and interactions are shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The C-terminal half of ECL2 in the X-ray structures forms a helical turn that caps the pocket and contributes side chains that interact with NECA (Phe168 and Glu169).
source: The C-terminal half of ECL2 in the X-ray structures forms a helical turn that caps the pocket and contributes side chains that interact with NECA (Phe168 and Glu169).
evidence: This is observed in the X-ray crystal structures.

claim: In the cryo-EM structure, the C-terminal half of ECL2 is more disordered.
source: In the cryo-EM structure this region is more disordered.
evidence: Disorder is inferred from poor density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: There is no significant side chain density for Phe168 and Glu169 in the cryo-EM map.
source: As a consequence, there is no significant side chain density for Phe168 and Glu169 in the cryo-EM map.
evidence: Lack of density is observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The fact that there is clear density for NECA and His264 excludes the possibility that the whole extracellular portion of the receptor is moving as a rigid body.
source: The fact that there is clear density for NECA and His264 excludes the possibility that the whole of this region has poor resolution that is the extracellular portion of the receptor is not moving as a rigid body.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of density quality in different regions.

claim: ECL2 is dynamic.
source: This is consistent with ECL2 being dynamic.
evidence: Dynamics is inferred from the variable density quality.

claim: The cryo-EM map suggests a rotamer for the imidazole group of His264 that points away from the orthosteric binding pocket.
source: Although the cryo-EM map in the region is poorer than in the rest of the molecule, it suggests a rotamer for the imidazole group of His264 that points away from the orthosteric binding pocket (Figure 6).
evidence: The rotamer is modeled based on the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 6.

claim: The ionic bridge between Glu169 and His264 affects small molecule binding kinetics.
source: This ionic bridge affects small molecule binding kinetics (Segala et al., 2016) and in most of the crystal structures caps the binding pocket.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The difference in His264 rotamer might be a consequence of the pH in which the respective structures were determined.
source: This might be a consequence of the pH in which the respective structures were determined.
evidence: This is speculated based on the pKa of histidine and pH conditions.

claim: The pKa of the histidine side chain is ~6.
source: The pKa of the histidine side chain is ~6 and most crystal structures have been obtained at lower pH (~pH 5), favouring protonation of His264 and the formation of the ionic bridge.
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge about histidine.

claim: At pH 7.5, His264 would be predominantly deprotonated and unable to form the ionic bridge.
source: At a more physiological pH of 7.5 that was used for the cryo-EM structure, His264 would be predominantly deprotonated and unable to form the ionic bridge.
evidence: This is inferred from the pKa of histidine and the pH used.

claim: In the physiological state (represented by the cryo-EM map) the ionic bridge between His264 and Glu169 is likely absent, unless the surrounding pH is momentarily lowered for specific functions.
source: Therefore, it is likely that in the physiological state (represented by the cryo-EM map) this ionic bridge is also absent, unless the surrounding pH is momentarily lowered for specific functions (e.g. the release of high concentrations of glutamate in glutamatergic synapses).
evidence: This is inferred from the pH dependence of the ionic bridge and speculated about physiological conditions.

claim: The interface between mini-GS in the heterotrimeric G protein and A2AR in the cryo-EM structure is very similar to the interface between mini-GS and A2AR in the X-ray structure (PDB code 5g53).
source: The interface between mini-GS in the heterotrimeric G protein and A2AR in the cryo-EM structure is very similar to the interface between mini-GS and A2AR in the X-ray structure (PDB code 5g53).
evidence: Similarity is determined from structural comparison.

claim: The interface in the cryo-EM structure has a buried surface of 1135 Å2 compared to 1048 Å2 for the X-ray structure 5g53.
source: The interface in the cryo-EM structure has a buried surface of 1135 Å2 compared to 1048 Å2 for the X-ray structure 5g53; the slight increase is due to interactions between ICL1 of A2AR (residues Leu110 and Asn113) and the N-terminal helix of mini-GS (residues His41 and Arg38).
evidence: Buried surface area is calculated from the structures.

claim: The slight increase in buried surface area is due to interactions between ICL1 of A2AR (residues Leu110 and Asn113) and the N-terminal helix of mini-GS (residues His41 and Arg38).
source: The interface in the cryo-EM structure has a buried surface of 1135 Å2 compared to 1048 Å2 for the X-ray structure 5g53; the slight increase is due to interactions between ICL1 of A2AR (residues Leu110 and Asn113) and the N-terminal helix of mini-GS (residues His41 and Arg38).
evidence: These interactions are observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The main interactions between A2AR and mini-GS in both the cryo-EM and X-ray structures are made predominantly by the C-terminal α5 helix in mini-GS and amino acid residues in H3, H5, H6, H7, H8 and ICL2 of A2AR.
source: The main interactions between A2AR and mini-GS in both the cryo-EM and X-ray structures are made predominantly by the C-terminal α5 helix in mini-GS and amino acid residues in H3, H5, H6, H7, H8 and ICL2 of A2AR (Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: Interactions are observed in both structures and supported by citation.

claim: The amino acid residues that make interactions between A2AR and mini-GS are identical in cryo-EM and X-ray structures, but the rotamers sometimes differ.
source: The amino acid residues that make these interactions are identical, but the rotamers sometimes differ between the cryo-EM and X-ray structures.
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: Differences in rotamers may be a reflection of the different chemical environments in which the structures were determined or the slight difference in curvature of the α5 helix in mini-GS.
source: This may be a reflection of the different chemical environments in which the structures were determined or the slight difference in curvature of the α5 helix in mini-GS.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed differences.

claim: Some interactions may be transient and are captured in one structure and not another.
source: In addition, some interactions may be transient and are captured in one structure and not another.
evidence: This is speculated to explain differences between structures.

claim: Arg291 at the intracellular end of H7 of A2AR adopts a different conformation in the cryo-EM structure compared to the crystal structure.
source: For example, Arg291 at the intracellular end of H7 of A2AR adopts a different conformation in the cryo-EM structure compared to the crystal structure.
evidence: Different conformations are observed in the two structures.

claim: The different conformation of Arg291 results in the absence of interactions between the Arg291 side chain and mini-GS.
source: This results in the absence of interactions between the Arg291 side chain and mini-GS, although the backbone carbonyl can still makes potential interactions with Glu392 and the adjacent residues in H8 are still sufficiently close to mini-GS to make interactions.
evidence: This is observed from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The region around Arg291 is the main difference to the β2AR-GS complex where the α5 helix in GS does not interact with H7 and H8 of the receptor.
source: This region is also the main difference to the β2AR-GS complex where the α5 helix in GS does not interact with H7 and H8 of the receptor (Rasmussen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with the cited structure.

claim: The major difference between the cryo-EM structure of the A2AR-heterotrimeric G protein complex and the X-ray structure of the A2AR-mini-GS complex was the presence of the βγ subunit.
source: The major difference between the structure determined by cryo-EM of the A2AR-heterotrimeric G protein complex and the X-ray structure of the A2AR-mini-GS complex was the presence of the βγ subunit in the cryo-EM structure.
evidence: This is a direct comparison of the two structures.

claim: No interactions were observed between A2AR and the γ subunit.
source: No interactions were observed between A2AR and the γ subunit, but potential interactions were observed between ICL1 (residues Ser35, Asn36 and Gln38) of A2AR and the β subunit (Arg52, Asp312, Asp333 and Phe335).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Potential interactions were observed between ICL1 (residues Ser35, Asn36 and Gln38) of A2AR and the β subunit (Arg52, Asp312, Asp333 and Phe335).
source: No interactions were observed between A2AR and the γ subunit, but potential interactions were observed between ICL1 (residues Ser35, Asn36 and Gln38) of A2AR and the β subunit (Arg52, Asp312, Asp333 and Phe335).
evidence: These interactions are observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The interface between A2AR and the β subunit is considerably more extensive than that observed in the β2AR complex, where interactions occur exclusively at Asp312.
source: This interface between A2AR and the β subunit is considerably more extensive than that observed in the β2AR complex (Figure 7), where interactions occur exclusively at Asp312.
evidence: Comparison is shown in Figure 7.

claim: ICL1 shows higher B-factors than the rest of the A2AR cryo-EM structure, which may suggest that the interaction is fairly weak.
source: However, ICL1 shows higher B-factors than the rest of the A2AR cryo-EM structure, which may suggest that the interaction is fairly weak.
evidence: Higher B-factors are observed in the refined structure, suggesting flexibility or weak interaction.

claim: The cryo-EM structures of the Class B Calcitonin receptor and Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor bound to heterotrimeric GS show a similar interaction between ICL1 and the β subunit where only Asp312 in the β subunit apparently interacts with ICL1 of the receptor.
source: The recently reported cryo-EM structures of the Class B Calcitonin receptor (Liang et al., 2017) and Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (Zhang et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2018) bound to heterotrimerc GS also show a similar interaction between ICL1 and the β subunit where only Asp312 in the β subunit apparently interacts with ICL1 of the receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with cited structures.

claim: The larger interface between the β subunit and A2AR appears at the moment unique to this receptor.
source: Therefore, the larger interface between the β subunit and A2AR appears at the moment unique to this receptor, although the physiological implications are unclear.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with other receptor structures.

claim: Contacts between A2AR and the heterotrimeric G protein were identified between ICL1 and the β subunit, and between ICL2 and part of the N-terminal α-helix of the α subunit.
source: Firstly, contacts between A2AR and the heterotrimeric G protein were identified between ICL1 and the β subunit, and between ICL2 and part of the N-terminal α-helix of the α subunit; these regions of the G protein were either absent or disordered, respectively, in the crystal structure.
evidence: These contacts are observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The difference in pH under which the cryo-EM structure was determined (pH 7.5) compared to many X-ray structures (pH <6) led to ECL2 being more dynamic, as the potential salt bridge between His264 and Glu169 was absent, and consequently Phe168 was disordered.
source: Secondly, the difference in pH under which the cryo-EM structure was determined (pH 7.5) compared to many X-ray structures (pH <6) led to ECL2 being more dynamic, as the potential salt bridge between His264 and Glu169 was absent, and consequently Phe168 was disordered.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in the structures and the pH conditions.

claim: There are now two Class A receptors whose structures have been determined coupled to heterotrimeric GS: β2AR and A2AR.
source: There are now two Class A receptors whose structures have been determined coupled to heterotrimeric GS, β2AR (Rasmussen et al., 2011) and A2AR, and after this work was completed, two Class B structures coupled to GS were also published (Liang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017; Liang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on the literature and the current work.

claim: The overall architecture of the receptors coupled to GS is conserved, but the details differ.
source: As expected the overall architecture of the receptors coupled to GS are conserved, but the details differ.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of multiple structures.

claim: The biggest difference between coupling of Class A receptors to Class B receptors is that the position of H8 in the Class B receptors is angled towards the G protein by ~30° compared to the Class A receptors.
source: The biggest difference between coupling of Class A receptors to Class B receptors is that the position of H8 in the Class B receptors is angled towards the G protein by ~30˚compared to the Class A receptors.
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: The angled position of H8 in Class B receptors results in extensive contacts between H8 and the G protein β subunit that are absent in Class A receptors.
source: This results in extensive contacts between H8 and the G protein β subunit that are absent in Class A receptors.
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: All the receptor structures coupled to GS show the majority of the contacts between the α5 helix of the α subunit and H3, H5 and H6 of the receptor, with receptor-dependent contacts in H2, H7 and H8.
source: All the receptor structures coupled to GS show the majority of the contacts between the α5 helix of the α subunit and H3, H5 and H6 of the receptor, with receptor-dependent contacts in H2, H7 and H8.
evidence: This is observed from comparison of multiple structures.

claim: The differences in contacts may arise partially from the subtle difference in bending of the C-terminal part of the α5 helix and the different positions of the α5 helix within the receptor.
source: The differences may arise partially from the subtle difference in bending of the C-terminal part of the α5 helix and the different positions of the α5 helix within the receptor, both presumably arising from the different amino acid sequences of the respective receptors.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural observations.

claim: The interactions observed between A2AR and the β subunit are also observed in the Class B receptors, but are absent from the crystal structure of the β2AR-GS structure.
source: The interactions observed here between A2AR and the β subunit are also observed in the Class B receptors, but are absent from the crystal structure of the β2AR-GS structure, although a shift of the β subunit by only a few ångstroms would be sufficient for interactions to occur.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of structures.

claim: A shift of the β subunit by only a few ångstroms would be sufficient for interactions to occur in β2AR.
source: The interactions observed here between A2AR and the β subunit are also observed in the Class B receptors, but are absent from the crystal structure of the β2AR-GS structure, although a shift of the β subunit by only a few ångstroms would be sufficient for interactions to occur.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural analysis.

claim: The poor density of ECL2 in the cryo-EM map of A2AR coupled to the heterotrimeric G protein suggests that this region is more dynamic than suggested from the X-ray structures.
source: The poor density of ECL2 in the cryo-EM map of A2AR coupled to the heterotrimeric G protein, suggests that this region is more dynamic than suggested from the X-ray structures, maybe due to a pH effect that breaks the salt bridge between His264 and Glu169.
evidence: Dynamics is inferred from poor density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The salt bridge between His264 and Glu169 has been suggested to be highly important in modulating the kinetics of ligand binding.
source: This salt bridge has been suggested to be highly important in modulating the kinetics of ligand binding (Segala et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: A recent structure of A2AR bound to compound-1 was crystallised at pH 6.5, and no crystal contacts were formed by ECL2.
source: Interestingly, a recent structure (Sun et al., 2017) of A2AR bound to compound-1 was crystallised at pH 6.5, and no crystal contacts were formed by ECL2.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In the structure of A2AR bound to compound-1, the N-terminal section of ECL2 lacked density and Phe168 adopts two conformations.
source: In this structure, the N-terminal section of ECL2 lacked density as we observed in the cryo-EM map and, in the latter region, Phe168 adopts two conformations.
evidence: This is observed in the cited structure.

claim: In one conformation of Phe168, it stacks against the ligand and in the other conformation Phe168 points towards the extracellular surface.
source: In one conformation, Phe168 stacks against the ligand and in the other conformation Phe168 points towards the extracellular surface (Figure 6).
evidence: This is observed in the cited structure and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The cryo-EM structure adds support to the contention that ECL2 is flexible and may be important in modulating the accessibility of the orthosteric binding site to ligands.
source: The cryo-EM structure thus adds support to the contention that ECL2 is flexible and may be important in modulating the accessibility of the orthosteric binding site to ligands.
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM observations and prior structural data.

claim: The cryo-EM structure allows for the first time a direct comparison of the structure of a GPCR bound to an identical ligand in the same conformation as determined by cryo-EM and X-ray crystallography.
source: The cryo-EM structure presented here allows for the first time a direct comparison of the structure of a GPCR bound to an identical ligand in the same conformation as determined by cryo-EM and X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is stated as a unique aspect of this work.

claim: Cryo-EM offers a relatively fast route to the structure of a GPCR in an active conformation coupled to the heterotrimeric G protein GS.
source: Cryo-EM offers a relatively fast route to the structure of a GPCR in an active conformation coupled to the heterotrimeric G protein GS.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of cryo-EM and crystallography workflows.

claim: The quality of most of the cryo-EM map was very similar to the electron density map from the X-ray structure, despite the reported resolutions being 4.1 Å and 3.4 Å, respectively.
source: The quality of most of the cryo-EM map was very similar to the electron density map from the X-ray structure, despite the reported resolutions being 4.1 Å and 3.4 Å, respectively.
evidence: This is observed from direct comparison of the maps.

claim: This highlights the importance of the local resolution vs the global resolution in cryo-EM maps.
source: This highlights the importance of the local resolution vs the global resolution in cryo-EM maps.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that map quality is similar despite different global resolutions.

claim: In both cryo-EM and X-ray structures, the ligand density was unambiguous.
source: In both cases, the ligand density was unambiguous, but adenosine is an asymmetric molecule and difficulties would have been encountered if the ligand was more symmetrical, such as caffeine.
evidence: This is observed in both structures.

claim: Difficulties would have been encountered if the ligand was more symmetrical, such as caffeine.
source: In both cases, the ligand density was unambiguous, but adenosine is an asymmetric molecule and difficulties would have been encountered if the ligand was more symmetrical, such as caffeine.
evidence: This is speculated based on the asymmetry of the ligand.

claim: Cryo-EM is preferred in terms of overall speed compared to X-ray crystallography.
source: However, there is no doubt that cryo-EM is preferred in terms of overall speed; extensive protein engineering is required to obtain crystals of GPCRs (Tate and Schertler, 2009), through adding fusion proteins, deletions of flexible regions, removal of post-translational modifications and thermostabilisation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of the two methods and supported by citation.

claim: Extensive protein engineering is required to obtain crystals of GPCRs.
source: However, there is no doubt that cryo-EM is preferred in terms of overall speed; extensive protein engineering is required to obtain crystals of GPCRs (Tate and Schertler, 2009), through adding fusion proteins, deletions of flexible regions, removal of post-translational modifications and thermostabilisation.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In theory, none of the protein engineering modifications required for crystallography will be required for a cryo-EM structure.
source: In theory, none of these modifications will be required for a cryo-EM structure, particularly as mild detergents, amphipols and nanodiscs are all compatible with structure determination of membrane proteins by cryo-EM and will maintain often quite unstable membrane proteins in a functional state (Tate, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical advantage and supported by citation.

claim: Once a crystal structure has been determined, they can often attain much higher resolution than structures of membrane proteins obtained by cryo-EM so far.
source: However, once a crystal structure has been determined, they can often attain much higher resolution than structures of membrane proteins obtained so far, although high-resolution cryo-EM structures are possible from single molecule imaging (Bartesaghi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of typical resolutions and supported by citation.

claim: High-resolution cryo-EM structures are possible from single molecule imaging.
source: However, once a crystal structure has been determined, they can often attain much higher resolution than structures of membrane proteins obtained so far, although high-resolution cryo-EM structures are possible from single molecule imaging (Bartesaghi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Another current advantage of X-ray crystallography is the possibility of soaking crystals to get multiple structures of a receptor bound to different ligands through molecular replacement.
source: Another current advantage of X-ray crystallography is the possibility of soaking crystals to get multiple structures of a receptor bound to different ligands through molecular replacement (Rucktooa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: There is still a size limitation of the molecule imaged by cryo-EM for structure determination and experimentally this is now at about 65 kDa.
source: Finally, there is still a size limitation of the molecule imaged by cryo-EM for structure determination (Henderson, 1995) and experimentally this is now at about 65 kDa (Khoshouei et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Given the continued drive towards improving the technology of cryo-EM, there is no doubt that this technique will play a pivotal role in structure-based drug design in future years.
source: However, given the continued drive towards improving the technology of cryo-EM, there is no doubt that this technique will play a pivotal role in structure-based drug design in future years (Vinothkumar and Henderson, 2016).
evidence: This is speculated based on current trends and supported by citation.
